cards.front: In a eukaryotic cell that sends out a protein, why does blocking one step stop the protein from reaching the later stops?
cards.back: Each cell part on the route can only work on what the part before it hands over, so nothing passes the block.
cards.quote: Each cell part on a route can only work on what the part before it hands over.

cards.front: In a pancreatic beta cell, list in order the parts insulin passes through, from the gene to release.
cards.back: A messenger RNA copy leaves the nucleus; ribosome on the rough ER; vesicle; Golgi apparatus; another vesicle that fuses with the cell membrane.
cards.quote: Then the protein travels: from a ribosome on the rough ER, by vesicle (a small bubble of membrane) to the Golgi apparatus

cards.front: A drug blocks protein from leaving the ER of a beta cell. Where does insulin build up at first, and what may happen over hours?
cards.back: It may build up in the ER, before the block, at first. Some may be broken down, and over hours the cell may make less.
cards.why: Protein already on the route piles up before a blocked handoff, because the next part cannot work on what it never receives.
cards.quote: If a handoff, such as leaving the ER or the Golgi, is blocked, protein already on the route may build up before the block at first.

cards.front: A drug stops the ribosomes of a beta cell from working. Does new insulin pile up anywhere on the route?
cards.back: No. No new insulin is made, so there is nothing to pile up.
cards.why: Blocking a handoff causes a pile-up; blocking the copy or the ribosome stops new protein being made.
cards.quote: Blocking the copy or the ribosome instead stops new protein being made.

cards.front: How does a ribosome building a new insulin chain end up at the ER?
cards.back: The first stretch of the chain is an address tag. A helper particle reads it and brings the ribosome to a channel in the ER membrane, and the chain grows into the ER.
cards.quote: The first stretch of a new insulin chain is an address tag.
cards.section: What the first film left out

cards.front: In a beta cell, how does the insulin precursor become insulin?
cards.back: In storage vesicles that leave the Golgi, cuts remove a middle stretch, leaving two short chains held together: insulin.
cards.quote: In the storage vesicles that leave the Golgi, cuts remove a middle stretch, leaving two short chains held together
cards.section: What the first film left out

cards.front: Besides paying for work, how does a rise in ATP in a beta cell lead to insulin release?
cards.back: It acts as a signal. It sets off a chain of events, passed on by calcium as a messenger, that makes more storage vesicles fuse with the cell membrane.
cards.quote: The rise sets off a chain of events, passed on by calcium acting as a messenger, that makes more storage vesicles fuse with the cell membrane and release insulin.
cards.section: What the first film left out

cards.front: Blood sugar rises, but a beta cell's mitochondria make much less ATP. Give two separate reasons insulin release would fall.
cards.back: 1) A smaller ATP rise, so a weaker signal to make storage vesicles fuse. 2) Steps that need energy, such as moving protein from the rough ER to the Golgi (shown in a 1968 follow-up on digestive-enzyme cells), slow down.
cards.why: Rests on two stated rules: the ATP rise is the release signal, and the route's moves need energy from ATP.
cards.quote: When blood sugar rises, more sugar enters a beta cell, and its mitochondria break the sugar down and make more ATP
cards.section: What the first film left out

cards.front: A drug stops vesicles from leaving the Golgi of a beta cell. Would the stuck protein be finished insulin or the longer precursor?
cards.back: Mostly the uncut precursor.
cards.why: The cuts that turn the precursor into insulin happen in storage vesicles that leave the Golgi, a stop the protein never reaches.
cards.quote: That chain is an insulin precursor, one chain longer than insulin.
cards.section: What the first film left out

cards.front: An {{c1::organelle}} is a structure inside a cell that does a particular job; most are wrapped in their own membrane.
cards.quote: An organelle is a structure inside a cell that does a particular job; most are wrapped in their own membrane.
cards.section: Parts on the route, and parts off it

cards.front: What is the main job of the Golgi apparatus?
cards.back: It sorts and packs proteins and sends them on.
cards.quote: Sorts and packs proteins and sends them on
cards.section: Parts on the route, and parts off it

cards.front: What is a lysosome, and is it usually found in plant cells, animal cells or both?
cards.back: A sac of digestive enzymes that breaks down worn-out cell parts. Animal cells; plant cells usually not, because the vacuole does similar digesting.
cards.quote: Sac of digestive enzymes that breaks down worn-out cell parts
cards.section: Parts on the route, and parts off it

cards.front: How do the jobs of rough ER and smooth ER differ?
cards.back: Rough ER, dotted with ribosomes, folds new proteins for export or for membranes. Smooth ER makes lipids.
cards.quote: rough ER, dotted with ribosomes, folds new proteins for export or for membranes, and smooth ER makes lipids
cards.section: Parts on the route, and parts off it

cards.front: Plant and animal cells share most structures. Which three do plant cells add?
cards.back: A cell wall, a large central vacuole and, in green cells, chloroplasts.
cards.quote: plant cells add a cell wall, a large central vacuole and, in green cells, chloroplasts
cards.section: Parts on the route, and parts off it

cards.front: The {{c1::cytoplasm}} is everything inside the cell membrane but outside the nucleus; many reactions happen there.
cards.quote: Everything inside the membrane but outside the nucleus; many reactions happen here
cards.section: Parts on the route, and parts off it

cards.front: A carrot root cell is not green and has no chloroplasts. Can it make ATP, and if so, which part does it?
cards.back: Yes. Its mitochondria release energy from sugar and store it in ATP.
cards.why: Mitochondria are found in both plant and animal cells; chloroplasts are a separate organelle for photosynthesis.
cards.quote: Release energy from sugar and store it in ATP
cards.section: Parts on the route, and parts off it

cards.front: In a model beta cell, the lysosomes are switched off. Does insulin still leave the cell? What might build up over days?
cards.back: Insulin still leaves, because lysosomes are not on its route. Worn-out cell parts might build up.
cards.quote: Switch off the lysosomes, which break down worn-out cell parts.
cards.section: Explore: test the one idea in a model

cards.front: A factory model calls mitochondria the cell's power plant. What does that picture get wrong?
cards.back: Mitochondria do not create energy. They move energy from sugar into ATP.
cards.quote: Mitochondria do not create energy; they move energy from sugar into ATP.
cards.section: A factory model, and where it breaks

cards.front: Pancreas digestive-enzyme cells get a 3-minute pulse of a radioactive building block, then a chase. Grains are counted over each cell part at later times. What did the timing of each part's peak show?
cards.back: New protein moves rough ER, then Golgi vesicles, then condensing vacuoles, then storage granules: each part's share peaks later than the part before it.
cards.quote: Each part's own share peaks later than the part before it
cards.section: How a marked batch really moves

cards.front: In the pulse-chase data, at 17 minutes of chase the rough ER held 37.6% of grains and the Golgi vesicles 37.5%. What does this near-tie show about how a marked batch moves?
cards.back: It moves as a spreading wave, not one parcel, so the largest share does not hop neatly from part to part.
cards.quote: A marked batch moves as a spreading wave, not one parcel.
cards.section: How a marked batch really moves

cards.front: Pulse-chase data: at 57 minutes of chase, condensing vacuoles held 35.8% of counted grains and storage granules 32.9%. The pulse lasted 3 minutes. What share did those two parts hold together, and how long after the pulse began was this?
cards.back: 35.8 + 32.9 = 68.7% of counted grains. Time: 3 + 57 = 60 minutes after the pulse began, because the chase starts when the pulse ends.
cards.quote: At 57 minutes of chase, which two parts held most of the counted grains?
cards.section: How a marked batch really moves

cards.front: A pulse-chase run on digestive-enzyme cells is repeated with a chemical that blocks the mitochondria's ATP making. Where would most marked protein stay?
cards.back: Over the rough ER. In a 1968 follow-up, such chemicals stopped proteins moving from the rough ER to the Golgi.
cards.why: The move needs energy; without it the protein cannot reach the stops after it.
cards.quote: Chemicals that blocked the mitochondria's ATP making stopped proteins moving from the rough ER to the Golgi.
cards.section: How a marked batch really moves

cards.front: A {{c1::prokaryotic}} cell has no nucleus and none of the membrane-bound organelles on the insulin route; bacteria and archaea are examples.
cards.quote: A prokaryotic cell has no nucleus and none of the membrane-bound organelles on this route
cards.section: Same jobs, simpler parts: prokaryotic cells

cards.front: In a prokaryotic cell, where is the DNA kept, and what is that region called?
cards.back: In an open region with no membrane around it, called the nucleoid.
cards.quote: In an open region with no membrane, the nucleoid
cards.section: Same jobs, simpler parts: prokaryotic cells

cards.front: A bacterium sends proteins out, yet it has no ER or Golgi. How does it do the job?
cards.back: Its ribosomes build the protein in the cytoplasm, and a channel in the cell membrane moves it across. In bacteria with an outer membrane, another channel or a system spanning both membranes is also needed.
cards.quote: Its ribosomes build the protein in the cytoplasm, and a channel in the cell membrane moves it across.
cards.section: Same jobs, simpler parts: prokaryotic cells

cards.front: What fits heart muscle cells holding many mitochondria (about 30% of cell volume in one study of normal mice)?
cards.back: Cells that need a large, steady supply of ATP made using oxygen often hold more mitochondria; the heart beats without rest.
cards.quote: Cells that need a large, steady supply of ATP made using oxygen often hold more mitochondria.
cards.section: Cells built for their work

cards.front: Normal Arabidopsis leaf cells held 121 chloroplasts on average; arc5 mutant cells held 13, each about six times larger. Treating six times larger as six normal chloroplasts' worth, compare the two by count and by amount.
cards.back: By count: 13 / 121 = about 11%. By amount, if size means volume, roughly: 13 x 6 = 78 normal-sized equivalents; 78 / 121 = about 64%. The count alone understates how much chloroplast is there.
cards.quote: each fully grown arc5 chloroplast was about six times larger, so the count alone understates how much chloroplast is there
cards.section: Cells built for their work

cards.front: The arc5 gene sits in the nucleus, yet changes how chloroplasts divide. What does this show about organelles?
cards.back: One organelle depends on another: the nucleus holds instructions that control the chloroplast.
cards.quote: The gene also shows one organelle depending on another: it sits in the nucleus, yet changes how chloroplasts divide.
cards.section: Cells built for their work

cards.front: Pancreas digestive-enzyme cells send out large amounts of protein. Using the rule that organelle amount often reflects a cell's work, predict which organelles they likely have plenty of, and why.
cards.back: Likely plenty of rough ER and Golgi, the parts that build, finish and ship exported protein, plus mitochondria to supply ATP for the moves. A prediction from the rule, not a measured amount.
cards.why: Extrapolates the stated rule (amount reflects work) to the export route; adds no new facts.
cards.quote: in eukaryotes the amount of an organelle often reflects the cell's work
cards.section: Cells built for their work

cards.front: Plan a light-microscope test of whether leaves grown in brighter light have more chloroplasts per cell. Name the independent variable, dependent variable, control, and one step that keeps the counting fair.
cards.back: Independent: light level. Dependent: chloroplasts per cell. Control: dim-light plants. Fairness: a partner codes the slides so the counter does not know the group; use one counting rule for every cell.
cards.quote: Do leaves grown in brighter light have more chloroplasts per cell? Plan an investigation with a light microscope.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Mitochondria filled 30.2% of heart muscle cell volume in normal mice and 18% of the whole liver's volume in normal rats. Why is this not a fair, matched comparison?
cards.back: Two things differ: the species (mice vs rats) and the measure (share of one cell type's volume vs share of the whole organ's volume).
cards.quote: Why is comparing 30.2% in heart cells with 18% in liver not a fair, matched comparison?
cards.section: Two more mitochondria numbers, and a fair test
